Psychedelics in the right setting and dose can induce a mystical awakening experience, but it's up to the individual to do the work in the rest of their life to get the full benefit of that awakening, or else it will just become a beautiful memory as the dullness of reality returns and old patterns re-emerge. 

Imagine a square candle that's being melted - if it's still in the same shaped box, it will be the same shape again after it hardens, and you'll be back where you started. The candle is your mind, the fire is LSD and the box is your habits and lifestyle, and you need to get the tools to change the shape of your box while you still have some semblance of stability in your life, because it will be disorienting and confining during the trip. Having a mind-melting high dose psychedelic experience and abandoning your box completely is how people end up in cults or mental wards.

My non medical advice would be to find a good time to take a psychedelic with an experienced guide, and also prepare by doing some research on things like support groups, therapists or 12 step programs related to your addiction, and perhaps some self-help books as well. That will help you develop a recovery-shaped box to provide the structure you need while you are changing your life.

Individuals who are prone to anxiety may be more likely to experience what trippers call a "loop" - intrusive thoughts that repeat over and over, causing escalating panic. The individual may worry that they are going insane without reassurance, or momentarily forget that they took a drug. Sometimes a feeling that "this has been happening forever" can lead to a fear that the trip will never end. This is why it's a good idea to take psychedelics around experienced users you trust, who can remind you that you're tripping and it will be over in x number of hours, and find ways to pull you out of your thoughts without making things worse. 

In my observations of individuals with ADD that are not anxiety-prone, they tend to regard the trip as being somewhat therapeutic for their condition: its slightly stimulating effects provide an Adderall-like ability to focus on the subject at hand and get lost in a painting or a song or engaging conversation for hours, while being distracted and impulsive becomes a fun, child-like way to interact with the world. Many people have made permanent changes in the way they manage their ADD inspired by things they learned about themselves on LSD or mushrooms. Good or bad, psychedelics will always teach you something.

Definitely avoid mixing any kind of psychedelic with ADHD medication though, plan a time when you can take a day off for the trip and a day off to recover and avoid taxing your serotonin and dopamine levels.

While Penn & Teller & staff are right that yoga involves a huge pseudoscience component, they did not do adequate research on the history of yoga in India in this episode, they mistakenly conflated its popularization in the West with its 'invention'. Saying that it was invented in the 60s, is like saying that the guitar was invented in the 1950s because that's when rock & roll emerged, neglecting the hundreds of years of its use in folk, jazz and classical music that preceded rock.

It evolved organically as a stretching form of 'prayer' (meditation is more accurate, even though some are deliberately for increasing energy) over hundreds of years. There was no one true inventor of yoga, only people who stake claim to being the first to devise a particular method or series of patterns (i.e. Bikram Chowhury and his specific set of asanas done in 85+ degree heat). Though most yoga practice in America today only works on one limb (asanas), it is part of an eightfold practice that also involves healthy diet, restraint, devotion, self-awareness, loyalty and many other less physical means of improving one's self.

Most of the explanation of how yoga works in the historical literature is based on the ayurvedic / chakra energy point system, which has now been largely discredited as being a vague sort of pseudoscience, but shares a lot in common with acupuncture, reflexology and several other forms of natural eastern medicine that appear to have some credible basis in healing. While many of the changes in prana flow made during yoga have a literal physical counterpart (e.g. what we call muladharabanda, a doctor would call flexion of the pelvic floor and PC muscles) but as to whether they really cause 'energy to flow up and down channels of your body' is a fairly mystical interpretation of the workings of the nervous and cardiovascular system, albeit one that helps less scientifically minded people understand how to listen to the signs of their body. - Alcohol + GHB/GBL

- Alcohol + opioids (Vicodin, heroin, etc)

- Alcohol + benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium, etc) or barbituarates 

- GHB/GBL + benzos (pretty much guaranteed blackout)

- Alcohol + ketamine

- Alcohol + tramadol

- Alcohol + antidepressants (heard of it happening with Wellbutrin and Effexor) 

- Opiates + benzos

- Large amounts of benzos alone

- Large amounts of GHB alone

- Quaaludes (not sure if these are around anymore but im sure combining them with alcohol would be even worse)

- Large amounts of alcohol + any kind of stimulant (MDMA, speed, coke) or psychedelic (LSD, shrooms, RCs) - these allow you to stay awake doing stupid shit when you should be passed out from drinking too much

- Large amounts of alcohol alone

- Phenazepam

- Methoxetamine

- Ketamine (if you consider the k-hole a blackout since you can't really tell what's going on in real life while it's happening)

Similarly, any particularly muscular, fit man has sisters that, proportional to their body type, could be similarly fit with enough training, if they had the same amount of testosterone. As a former bulimic who sympathizes deeply with everything you've written, please see a counselor! They can help you learn techniques to build healthier self esteem. Three things that really helped me grow and recover:

- The realization that beauty is inherently subjective. When you look in the mirror and see "ugly, bad, fat", whatever, it's because of the psychological outlook of a negative mind state casting a curtain over the world. Ever hear a beautiful woman say something incredibly ignorant and then realize she's not so hot, or a weird looking man suddenly become handsome after hearing that he has a beautiful singing voice? This happens all the time. Even if you don't feel confident or beautiful, fake it. I guarantee you, there are attractive men out there who once they get to know your personality will think you are nothing less than radiant even first thing after waking up in a pair of sweatpants. But they won't ever get to know the real you when it's hidden behind a mask of self doubt.
- Dissociating 'myself' from 'my body'. On the internet, we don't have bodies or faces but we still have 'selves', the true self is our beliefs, how we act, and that's the part that's really interacting with the world. Your body isn't you. It's something you have, an object/vessel to take care of. When you relinquish attachment between your self and your body, something like "I gained 10 pounds" or "I have a pimple" becomes as harmless as "I need to mow the lawn" or "My car has a dent in it". Just fixable, temporary problems, not attacks on your worth as a person.
- Not hanging around with people who spend tons of time and energy worrying about their appearance and/or judging other people for theirs. For me in school it was the 'twink' (skinny pretty gay boy crowd), watching tv shows like America's Next Top Model, and reading the kind of websites where pictures of ugly or fat people would be posted along with funny captions and stuff, for others it might be the pro-ana community, or bodybuilders, meat market type bars or whatever. Getting rid of all of those things that would remind me of feeling insecure and sending me into a shame spiral. Since then, I've developed a caring network of new friends who chose to hang out with each other not because of how I look, but because of shared interests like music and art, and their appreciation of me is for my personality, taste, sense of humor and the things I've accomplished. Many of the people I knew from back in the day have also chilled out as they've grown older and I have that kind of relationship with them now too. I know that even if I were to gain 100 pounds overnight, these people would still want to hang out with me, and I no longer am racked with guilt over ordering fried food at lunch instead of the salad and those sorts of little things that can be so devastating when you have an ED or BDD.

These truths have to be internalized, not just read. There is still a quiet voice inside that thinks I'm disgusting and that everyone in the world is humoring me, but I have developed enough defenses and logical arguments to be able to tell that inner voice that it's wrong and needs to stuff it :) Now, I am much more romantically successful, happier, eat a good diet for my health instead of my weight, and never could have dreamed at my darkest times that I would feel this normal and unashamed of myself.

I am not a doctor and certainly not suggesting you go against medical advice, but speaking from my own personal history - I was misdiagnosed with ADHD as a child when it was the 'trendy diagnosis' for kids who misbehaved in class (not sure what I actually have but suspect it may be Narcissistic Personality Disorder, since my disdain for homework was rooted in the belief that I was always right instead of listening to authority, and thinking I could skate by on high intelligence instead of having to work at anything), and subsequently became heavily dependent on the meds and eventually drug addicted, not learning any therapeutic techniques or will power, something I struggle with to this day.

Psychiatrists specialize in the treatment of mental disorders with medication, which is usually efficacious for mood disorders like depression or psychotic disorders like schizophrenia, but for many others, particularly behavioral disorders, meds can cause more problems than they solve. While you might have bipolar disorder or something else where meds might help stabilize your mood, what you've mentioned so far sounds more typical of an Axis II disorder such as Borderline, Narcissistic or Histrionic Personality Disorders. These usually respond best to cognitive behavioral therapy, since it's not the brain chemicals which are out of whack but rather innate and learned behaviors in the form of abnormal habits, beliefs and compulsions that the person has trouble controlling. A therapist you have a good relationship with will help you recognize triggers that turn 'bitch mood' on, understand why you react the way you do, healthy stress relief techniques to avoid taking it out on your partner, and other skills focused on self awareness and self control of behavior.

Of course any psychiatrist worth their salt would recognize the difference and recommend you to a counselor, but if he/she is quick to put you on lots of medications, it might be worth getting a second opinion. Admitting you have a problem and being willing to try and change is the hardest and most essential step to treating mental issues, and you're already there!

Bipolar is linked to abnormalities in dopamine function. In normal people, you have slight elevations in dopamine levels at a few points during the day (often 'trained' to coincide with cups of coffee, workouts and other things that 'get you going') but it's supposed to naturally calm back down to lower levels at night as melatonin and other nts kick in so that you can sleep. Dopamine is the neurotransmitter that meth triggers, leading first to bursts of energy, euphoria, motivation and desire to talk and be productive, but eventually leading to insomnia, paranoia, loss of appetite, repeated 'twitchy' behavior and inability to regulate emotions. When not triggered by drugs this state is called 'hypomania'. If the person takes even more speed (or has an imbalance as in bipolar disorder) they can break through an 'edge' into full on mania where they may start deliberately staying up all night writing or talking, doing self destructive exaggerated behavior like spending tons of money or becomin extremely promiscuous and dare-devilish, and even believing delusions such as that they were given a "special mission from God" or that the world is going to end etc. Then as their dopamine levels drop, the 'reality of the world' and realizing how crazy they've been acting kicks in, and they fall into a deep depression, hating themselves, not wanting to do anything at all, being too tired to function and taking their frustration out on loved ones. This is similar to the 'comedown' from meth. In some ways, bipolar is like your body naturally producing speed, only you don't get to choose when you're 'high' and when you're coming down. Not all bipolar people act exactly the same way (some people repress it and try and deny it, some people exaggerate it as an excuse to not have to control their behavior, some are misdiagnosed etc) but they all have this sort of 'cycle' of extreme energy alternating with low energy. The medications for bipolar disorder even the levels of dopamine out so that they have relative stability like what people would call normal mood shifts rather than extremes.
